what_its_for: Afatinib is a cancer medicine used to treat a type of lung cancer called non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). It works specifically in patients whose cancer has certain gene changes (called EGFR mutations). It helps slow or stop cancer cells from growing by blocking signals that tell them to multiply.
how_to_take: Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. Do NOT crush, chew, or split the tablet. Take it on an EMPTY stomach — at least 1 hour before eating or 3 hours after eating. Try to take it at the same time every day to keep a steady level of medicine in your body.
dosing: The usual starting dose is 40 mg once daily. Your doctor may adjust your dose (up to 50 mg or down to 20 mg) based on how well you tolerate the medicine and any side effects you experience. Always follow exactly what your doctor tells you.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — BUT only if there are more than 12 hours until your next scheduled dose. If it is less than 12 hours until your next dose, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. NEVER take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store afatinib tablets at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep them away from heat, moisture, and direct sunlight. Store in the original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Do not store in the bathroom.
what_to_avoid: Avoid eating for at least 1 hour before and 3 hours after taking your dose. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice, as they can affect how the medicine works in your body. Avoid taking certain other medicines without talking to your doctor first, especially some antifungals (like ketoconazole), antibiotics (like rifampin), seizure medicines, or blood thinners. Tell ALL your doctors and pharmacist about every medicine, vitamin, supplement, or herbal product you take. Avoid becoming pregnant — use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 2 weeks after your last dose.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: severe or worsening diarrhea (more than 4 loose stools per day), signs of a serious skin reaction (blistering, peeling, painful rash, sores in your mouth), trouble breathing or shortness of breath, new or worsening cough, fever (temperature over 100.4°F or 38°C), eye problems such as redness, pain, or vision changes, signs of liver problems (yellowing of skin or eyes, dark urine, severe tiredness, stomach pain), or severe nausea and vomiting that you cannot control.
when_it_works: Afatinib starts working in your body right away after your first dose, but it may take several weeks before you or your doctor notice changes in your cancer. Your doctor will monitor your progress with regular check-ups, blood tests, and imaging scans. Do not stop taking this medicine on your own even if you feel well — always talk to your doctor first.
special_populations: Pregnancy and Breastfeeding: Afatinib can harm an unborn baby. Do not use if you are pregnant. Women of childbearing age must use effective contraception during treatment and for at least 2 weeks after the last dose. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine and for at least 2 weeks after the last dose. Kidney or Liver Problems: If you have severe kidney or liver disease, your doctor may need to adjust your dose or monitor you more closely. Tell your doctor about any kidney or liver conditions before starting this medicine. Older Adults: Older patients may be more sensitive to side effects, especially diarrhea and skin reactions. Report any new symptoms to your doctor promptly.
